title.narrative: GCAMF Refugees Financial Inclusion Guarantee Program 2019-2022
GCAMF Refugees Financial Inclusion Guarantee Program 2019-2022

description.narrative:
Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF) har tillsammans med UNHCR ansökt om finansiering från Sida om 30 816 003 SEK, budget för teknisk assistans (TA) samt subventionsgaranti både för administration och förväntad förlust, för att genomföra "Programmet för finansiellt inkluderande av flyktingar och värdsamhällen i Uganda" under perioden 2019-2024. Insatsen, som har initierats gemensamt av UNHCR och Sida, syftar till att förbättra försörjningen och motståndskraften för flyktingar och värdsamhällen genom ekonomisk inkludering och ökade försörjningsmöjligheter för flyktingar och värdsamhällen. Detta ska uppnås genom att: 1) främja egenföretagande och inkomstgenererande aktiviteter genom stöd till nystartade företag och utvidgning av befintlig affärsverksamhet genom mikrokreditlån; 2) förbättra flyktingars affärsförmåga och finansiella kunskaper genom tillhandahållande av icke-finansiella tjänster; 3) underlätta flyktingars sysselsättning genom att stödja småföretagens utlåning bland värdbefolkningen i de sektorer där flyktingar, i enlighet med landets lagar, kan anställas.
Programmet har i allmänhet en marknadsbaserad ansats som involverar partnerskap med en specialiserad mikrofinansieringsfond, stiftelsen GCAMF, som kommer att tillhandahålla skuldfinansiering till ett antal leverantörer av finansiella tjänster (Financial Service Providers- FSPer) som är villiga att låna ut till flyktingar. Stiftelsen kommer att tillförsäkras en partiell kreditgaranti från Sida som kommer att tillämpas om FSPerna inte kan fullgöra sina åtaganden som följd av att låntagare inte kunnat återbetala sina lån. Programmet har också en mekanism för teknisk assistans (TA).
Även om interventionen är ett gemensamt initiativ från UNHCR och Sida, är UNHCR inte den huvudsakliga samarbetspartnern för Sida - UNHCR har dock varit, och kommer att vara, en viktig partner i utformningen, planeringen och genomförandet av projektet. Den formella samarbetspartnern är GCAMF, en stiftelse registrerad i Luxemburg i september 2008, vars uppgift är att bidra till kampen mot fattigdom. GCAMF valdes ut genom ett öppet ansökningsförfarande för mikrofinansieringsfonder som genomfördes av UNHCR redan 2017. Därefter beställde Sida en översyn av GCAMFs interna styrnings- och kontrollsystem. Granskningen genomfördes av KPMG 2017 vars övergripande bedömning var att organisationen har den nödvändiga kapaciteten, kompetensen och systemen för genomförandet av insatsen. I samråd med UNHCR och Sida har GCAMF även identifierat tre finansiella tjänsteleverantörer (FSPer) som de viktigaste genomförande partnerna för projektet i Uganda: BRAC Uganda, VisionFund Uganda och Ugafode. Utbildningar i finansiell kompetens och affärsutveckling kommer också att tillhandahållas av icke-statliga organisationer (NGOer) som har den kompetens och erfarenhet som uppgiften kräver. VisionFund Uganda och BRAC Uganda har NGO-grenar som har erfarenhet av att tillhandahålla sådan utbildning och kapacitetsuppbyggnad. Ugafode FSP kommer att samarbeta med Jesuit Refugee Service (JSR) för att tillhandahålla dessa tjänster. Urvalet av NGOer gjordes av GCAMF och FSPerna i samråd med UNHCR och Sida.
Den totala budgeten för insatsens TA-mekanism är 61 101 746 kr, varav Sida bidrar med 27 094 351 kr (exkl. subventionsbeloppet för förväntad förlust på 2 290 122 kr) och de återstående 34 007 395 kr täcks av FSPerna. Cirka 22 924 229 kr av insatsbudgeten kommer att kanaliseras av GCAMF till FSPerna och 4 170 122 kr kommer att gå till GCAMF direkt.

Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF), in coordination with UNHCR, has applied to Sida for funding of 30,816,003 SEK, TA budget and subsidy for the guarantee, to carry out the financial inclusion program for refugees and host communities in Uganda during the period 2019-2024. The intervention, which has been initiated jointly by Sida and UNHCR, aims at improving livelihoods and resilience of refugees and host communities through financial inclusion and increased livelihood options for refugees and host communities, by: 1) fostering self-employment and income generating activities by supporting start-ups and expansion of existing business activities through micro-credit loans; 2) enhancing refugees' business skills and financial literacy through the provision of non-financial services; 3) facilitating refugees’ employment by supporting small businesses lending among the host population in those sectors where refugees, in accordance with the country´s laws, can be employed.
The program generally follows a market-based approach which involves partnering with a specialized micro-finance foundation, the GCAMF, which will provide debt funding to a number of financial service providers (FSPs) willing to lend to refugees. The Foundation will be recipient of a partial credit guarantee from Sida which will be used in case the FSPs default due to borrowers not being able of repaying back their loan. The program also has a Technical Assistance (TA) facility.
While the intervention is a joint initiative of Sida and UNHCR, UNHCR is not the main cooperation partner though it has been and remains to be an essential partner in the design, planning as well as implementation of the project. The formal cooperation partner is Grameen Crédit Agricole Microfinance Foundation (GCAMF), a Foundation registered in Luxembourg in September 2008. The mission of the Foundation is to contribute to the fight against poverty. GCAMF was selected through a call for applications for microfinance funds that was conducted by UNHCR back in 2017. Subsequently, Sida commissioned a review of its internal management and control system. The review was conducted by KPMG in 2017 and its overall assessment was that the organization has the necessary capacity, competencies and systems for the implementation of the intervention. In consultation with UNHCR and Sida, GCAMF has also identified three financial service providers (FSPs): BRAC Uganda, VisionFund Uganda, and UGAFODE as main implementing partners of the project in Uganda. Financial literacy and business development trainings will also be provided by NGOs who have the competency and the experience the task demands. VisionFund Uganda and BRAC Uganda have NGO wings that have experience in providing such training and capacity building services. Ugafode FSP will work with the Jesuit Refugee Service (JSR) to provide these services. The selection of the NGOs was done by GCAMF and the FSPs in consultation with UNHCR and Sida.
The intervention’s total budget of the TA facility of the program is 61,101,746 SEK, out of which Sida contributes 27,094,351 SEK (excl. the subsidy amount of 2,290,122 SEK) and the remaining 34,007,395 is contributed by the FSPs. Approximately 4,170,122 SEK of the intervention budget will be kept by GCAMF while approximately 22,924,229 SEK will be forwarded from GCAMF to the FSPs.

The overall objective of the intervention is to contribute to the protection and solutions of UNHCRs persons of concern and host populations by improving their livelihoods and self-reliance through the facilitation of access to credit for business activities.
The main expected short-term outcomes of the intervention are: - increased refugees access to financial services. - Improved financial understanding, budget management and business skills. - Increased business activities and turnover. - Increased employment among refugees and host community population.
As a long-term outcome, the program expects the target communities to have better ability to cope with risks and reduced vulnerability with an ultimate aim of decreasing poverty levels among the beneficiaries. This is also expected to bring down the level of aid dependency among refugees. The intervention will also help in creating incentives for lending of bank funds in protracted refugee situations, and it is hoped to help in freeing up and allowing more resources including donor funding to be spent on acute refugee needs. In terms of beneficiaries, the program plans to benefit 55 000 refugees and 51 000 host community members in intervention focus areas.

GCAMF has provided Sida with annual financial, narrative and audit reports in accordance with the agreement, alongside semi-annual narrative reports, albeit with significant delays when it comes to the submission of audit reports.
Throughout the implementation period, GCAMF reports that the financial service providers (FSPs) reached a total of 118,973 refugees and Ugandans with loans against a total target of 106,000 people. Out of the 118,973 people reached with financial services, 21,871 were refugees while 97,102 were from the host community. GCAMF and the FSPs thus reached 40% of the original target of having 55,000 refugees access financial services (in the form of loans). Meanwhile, the number of Ugandan borrowers (97,102) represents a significant overachievement - i.e. a 190% achievement against target - since the goal was for 51,000 Ugandans to access financial services. The overall results in terms of the number of loans issued is deemed satisfactory considering that the budget for technical assistance was not fully utilised as a consequence of Sida's decision to withhold the last tranche and the utilisation rate for the guarantee itself was only at 18.3 per cent. Moreover, the total results achieved are deemed satisfactory in light of the significant impact of the Covid-19 pandemic and associated restrictions had on the programme during the inception phase and on the socio-economic conditions in the refugee settlements.
As Sida has previously observed, the level of results achieved differs significantly between the three FSPs, and it is VisionFund Uganda (VFU) that accounts for the overwhelming majority of the results achieved. Throughout the entire implementation period, VFU issued loans to 108,789 individuals (i.e. 91% of the total number of borrowers reached, and 84% of all refugees reached). VFU thus achieved significantly better results compared to the other FSPs, and widely surpassed the target initially set for VFU. This is despite the fact that they did not fully leverage the chance to secure loans from GCAMF that were covered by Sida's guarantee. It is clear that VFUs approach providing group loans to refugees and individual loans to Ugandans, combined with the increased use of digital tools in its business operations has been the key factor behind this intervention reaching its overall targets. This approach helped spread the risk among group borrowers but also helped mitigate the impact of Know Your Customer (KYC) requirements that was a factor that contributed to delayed lending among the other FSPs. Moreover, the development and use of digital tools for loan management helped VFU's officers process applications and manage the loan portfolio efficiently.
The largest FSP participating in the programme - Brac Uganda Finance Limited (BUFL)- was originally assessed to be in the best position to leverage the guarantee instrument alongside Sida's technical assistance to the NGO counterpart, BRAC Foundation, to scale up its lending to refugees and host communities. However, BRAC suffered a significant deterioration in its loan portfolio quality following the outbreak of Covid-19 and this contributed to making BRAC more risk averse and restrictive in terms of granting loans in the refugee hosting areas. Brac did not request a loan from GCAMF that was covered by Sida's guarantee. Identifying that Brac was unlikely to reach the intended targets in terms of loans issued to both refugees and Ugandans was the reason why GCAMF proposed, and Sida accepted, a re-programming of the programme budget towards VFU and UGAFODE in July 2022.
Another area were results differed among the FSPs was the proportion of women among their clients. Women constituted 76% of all borrowers in the programme. However, 92% of BRACs borrowers were women and 74% of VFU's borrowers were women, while UGAFODE had a much lower share of women among its clients (24%). This information was largely presented without further explanation or analysis in the reports submitted, despite requests from Sida to do so, but Sida's conclusion is that the different business models among the FSPs and prioritising different segments of the refugee population largely explains these differences.
Interestingly, Sida observes that refugees were granted higher loan amounts (129 euros) than Ugandans (73 euros) on average, but GCAMF cannot explain which market mechanisms or business considerations among the FSPs contributed to this. Sida also notes that the average loan size differed substantially between the lenders. UGAFODE, which almost exclusively lent to refugees, had an average loan size of 413 euros, compared with 210 euros at Brac and as low as 37 euros at VFU. Sida's assessment is that these differences are primarily explained by the FSPs different business models and target groups. Whereas UGAFODE primarily targeted refugees with more established small and medium-sized enterprises, VFU issued many group loans that result in lower amounts per borrower.
Moreover, it shall be noted that the large number of new borrowers (41,624 people) in the fourth and final year of the programme (1 November 2022 - 31 October 2023) was somewhat unexpected given the fact that the FSPs could not use the full technical assistance budget because of Sida's decision to withhold the disbursement of the final tranche due to recurring delays to the submission of an annual audit report. Although the number of refugee borrowers were expected to be lower in the final year of the programme, when comparing to the host population, due to to previously observed trends in the reported loan data, Sida noted that the number of borrowers with refugee status amounted to only 434 people during the final year. This is primarily explained by the FSPs expressing a need to consolidate high quality portfolios with a lower risk of defaulting loans, with refugees deemed a higher-risk segment of the target population.
It shall be noted that it was consistently reported that there was a perception among the FSPs that lending to refugees was associated with higher risks in terms of non-repayment, either through defaulting on the loan re-payment schedule or as a result of the borrower returning to their country of origin. This was cited as another factor that contributed to a lower number of loans being issued to refugees than originally planned. Although the indicators used to measure loan portfolio quality (i.e. the PAR30 measurement) indicated that there was a slightly higher risk in lending to refugees, the difference between refugee and host community PAR30 performance continued to decrease throughout the activity period and was near identical at the end of the programme. This improvement is likely and partially explained by the consolidation of the FSPs' respective loan portfolios in the final year of the programme, with very few new loans issued to refugees, but it also indicates that there was a higher-degree of risk aversion for lending to refugees among the FSPs despite the availability of Sida's guarantee that was meant to lower the risk of doing so. Despite previously identified trends in loan data, the low proportion of refugee borrowers in the final year of the programme was somewhat unexpected considering the reported improvements in refugee loan repayment rates and ongoing dialogue with GCAMF and FSPs where it was emphasised that lending to the refugee population has shown proof of concept.
As stated above, the overarching objective of the programme was to contribute to the protection and solutions of UNHCRs persons of concern and host populations by improving their livelihoods and self-reliance through the facilitation of access to credit for business activities. With 21,871 refugees accessing loans directly or through group lending throughout the programme, alongside 97,102 members of host communities, there was significant improvement in access to financial services among refugees. Moreover, 7,404 refugees and 33,208 Ugandans opened savings accounts throughout the programme period, which is also lower than the planned targets outlined in the programme document.
Despite the lower than planned results, it is possible to ascertain that the programme has contributed to the first short-term objective of increasing access to financial services among refugees (albeit at a lower scale than planned). However, the results are assessed to be overall satisfactory despite the lower than planned achievements as these can be explained by a variety of factors such as the Covid-19 pandemic and its socio-economic impact, reductions in general food assistance for refugees that heightened vulnerabilities among the overall refugee population, and the low utilisation of the guarantee-covered loans by the FSPs. Moreover, Sida's decision to withhold the last tranche of technical assistance funding due to delayed reporting also likely to have reduced the ability of the FSPs to further scale up lending to refugees in the final year of the programme.
Throughout the programme, Sida consistently observed that the narrative reports remained focused on output level results such as the number of borrowers, savers and participants in different training sessions. GCAMF failed to include indicators and routinely capture and report outcome level data that showed improvements in financial literacy, budget management and business skills, increased level of business activities and turnover, or the impact on employment figures among the target groups. Although the mid-term evaluation report showed promising data among those accessing loans and financial services - in terms of the number of jobs created and improvements in household income levels and business activity - the annual narrative reports did not contain the same type of outcome level reporting. It is therefore difficult to assess to which extent the programme contributed to longer-term outcomes, such as the refugees' self-reliance and livelihoods, with the ultimate aim of reducing poverty levels, vulnerabilities, and aid dependency among the beneficiaries.
Lastly, it should be noted that fluctuations in humanitarian funding for the refugee response in Uganda did result in several reductions to the size of general food assistance provided to refugees (distributed in-kind or as cash assistance) during the programme activity period. A system for differentiated food assistance based on household factors was also launched by UNHCR and WFP towards the end of the programme period, which based on field visits and dialogue with refugees, UNHCR, WFP and others are assessed as having impacted refugee households access to food. As reported separately by UNHCR and other actors, reductions in humanitarian assistance resulted in heightened vulnerabilities among refugees and led to increased use of harmful coping mechanisms such as the sale of households assets, child labour and informal borrowing to afford basic goods, food, shelter and/or school-related costs. Although such circumstances make a reduction to perceived aid dependency a more difficult undertaking, the lack of outcome level data in the reports submitted by GCAMF makes it difficult to assess whether the programme contributed to reducing vulnerabilities and the impact of reductions in general food assistance among those participating in this programme.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
